title: Electrochemical Technologies for Cement Clinker Synthesis in the Context of Carbon Neutrality: Principles, Applications, and Progress
abstract: Clinker production accounts for approximately 7–8% of global anthropogenic CO₂ emissions, of which about 60% originates from the process emissions of limestone decomposition. These emissions can hardly be eliminated by conventional energy-efficiency measures, so achieving carbon neutrality calls for transformative production technologies. Electrochemical technologies employ electrons as clean reagents to achieve the directional conversion of substances under ambient conditions and have been validated industrially in chlor-alkali production, water electrolysis, and lithium-ion batteries. Based on an analysis of the structural dilemmas faced by the cement industry in energy consumption, environmental pollution, and carbon emissions, this paper introduces the fundamentals and core advantages of electrochemical technologies and reviews their applications in cement clinker synthesis. It covers the reaction mechanisms of low-temperature pH-gradient electrolysis, high-temperature molten-salt electrolysis, electrochemical conversion of silicate minerals, and direct electrosynthesis of active phases, as well as the evolution of cement electrolyzer configurations and key materials. The application prospects are assessed through life-cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis, and industrialization cases. The electrochemical route can reduce carbon emissions by more than 75% and even achieves carbon negativity when coupled with non-carbonate silicate feedstocks, representing a transformative direction for the deep decarbonization of the cement industry.

title: Supramolecular Viscoelastic Systems for Next-Generation Electronic Packaging and Soft Electronics: Assembly, Rheology, Electro-Thermal Transport, and PFAS- and Microplastic-Free Sustainability
abstract: Modern electronic packaging and soft electronic architectures face a converging engineering and environmental imperative: sustaining reliable dielectric insulation, capacitive coupling, mechanical compliance, and high-flux thermal dissipation under escalating power densities, while phasing out environmentally persistent per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and non-reworkable crosslinked polymers that generate secondary microplastics across the electronic waste lifecycle. Supramolecular viscoelastic systems—constructed from reversible non-covalent interactions including directional hydrogen bonding, electrostatic coacervation, host–guest inclusion, amphiphilic self-assembly, and dynamic ionic or metal–ligand coordination—offer an intelligent, adaptive materials platform capable of bridging this gap. By decoupling processing rheology from in-service structural stability, these stimuli-responsive networks span a continuous spectrum from shear-thinning viscoelastic fluids and bicontinuous mesophases to clay-like, strain-stiffening yield-stress solids. This review synthesizes recent advances (predominantly 2024–2026) across the structure–property–sustainability continuum of supramolecular viscoelastic systems for electronics. We examine molecular design rules and mesoscale assembly pathways, linear and nonlinear rheological dynamics under multi-stimuli actuation, broadband dielectric dispersion and capacitive gap filling, phonon-mediated thermal transport and adaptive thermal interface materials (TIMs), and circularity strategies for PFAS and microplastics elimination under Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design (SSbD) frameworks. Key reliability bottlenecks—including moisture stability, DC breakdown strength, high-temperature creep resistance, and scalable solvent-free processing—are delineated to guide industrial qualification.

title: Hydrophobic Interaction as the Resolution of Interfacial Frustration
abstract: The hydrophobic effect is a solvent-mediated phenomenon in aqueous molecular systems, with consequences for liquid interfaces, self-assembly, polymer collapse and protein organisation. Contemporary statistical-mechanical frameworks explain much of its thermodynamics, including the dependence of hydration on solute size, density fluctuations and interfacial formation. The remaining conceptual challenge is not the absence of successful theories, but the lack of a common spatial language for describing how heterogeneous non-polar interfaces perturb the collective state of water. In this paper, I propose interfacial frustration as such a descriptor: a spatially distributed representation of the mismatch between the statistically preferred state of interfacial water and the geometric constraints imposed by a non-polar interface. Hydrophobic association is considered as a solvent-mediated reorganisation and, in appropriate cases, a reduction or redistribution of this mismatch, while retaining the established thermodynamic description in terms of free energy (G), enthalpy (H), entropy (S) and density fluctuations. The framework is intended as a complementary representation, not a replacement for existing theories such as Lum-Chandler-Weeks (LCW) theory. A component-resolved operational representation is specified, and its potential application to water–n-alkane interfaces and aqueous polymer collapse is developed as a proposed analytical programme. A more tentative extension to protein dynamics is also retained. These applications are proposed tests, not empirical validation of the framework. Its value depends on whether the spatial pattern and non-additivity of interfacial frustration provide predictive information beyond established surface-area, density, intermolecular-interaction and conformational-ensemble descriptors
